mainTopic: Responsibility for goring oxen held by others: guardians of a חרש, שוטה, or קטן, the nature and amount of כופר, and a borrower whose ox turns out to be a מועד.
overview: This amud covers three topics. First, it finishes discussing רבי יעקב's ruling about the ox of a חרש, שוטה, or קטן. The ruling could be about a תם, which would teach that בית דין appoints an אפוטרופוס. רבא's reading as a מועד is defended because it packs two ideas into one case. רבינא then says the real argument is whether a change of control (רשות משנה) turns a מועד back into a תם. Next, a ברייתא says stewards do not pay כופר. רב חסדא and רב פפא debate whether כופר is atonement or a money payment, and whose value sets the amount. Then רב אחא בר יעקב asks רב נחמן two hard questions about כופר: how partners pay it, and whether בית דין takes collateral for it. רב נחמן cannot answer. Last, a ברייתא about a borrowed ox that turns out to be a מועד leads to a back-and-forth about why the borrower still pays half. That debate continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The ruling could be about a תם ox
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows two ways the ברייתא could be talking about a תם that was not guarded well enough: one according to רבי יהודה and one according to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you follow רבי יהודה, the case is where the guardian gave the ox only reduced guarding and not superior guarding. If you follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, the case is where he gave it no guarding at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is pushing back on רבא's claim that the case must be a מועד. It shows that the case could just as easily be a תם that was not guarded properly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a תם to be liable at all, the guarding must have failed. According to רבי יהודה, reduced guarding is not enough for this ox, so the case is reduced guarding without superior guarding. According to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, even reduced guarding is enough, so the case must be one with no guarding at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Reduced or basic guarding, such as a simple rope or ordinary door.
Superior or excellent guarding.
An ox with no history of goring. Its owner pays half damage, collected only from the ox itself.
An ox that has been warned after goring repeatedly. Its owner pays full damage.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the גמרא is changing the law here. It is only showing that the same ברייתא could fit a תם, depending on which opinion about guarding you follow.

phrases.english: If according to Rabbi Yehuda —
it is a case where he gave it reduced guarding,
and did not give it superior guarding.
If according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov —
it is a case where he did not guard it at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the challenge against רבא (from the previous part of the daf), who said רבי יעקב's ruling must be about a מועד.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's explanation that רבי יעקב's ruling of חצי נזק is about a מועד.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A workable case of a תם exists under both major views about guarding, so there is no need to explain the ruling as a מועד.

steps.title: Source for רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's view
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא proves that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב holds that reduced guarding is enough for both a תם and a מועד.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says that for both a תם and a מועד, if the owner gave them reduced guarding, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source showing why, according to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, the case has to be one with no guarding at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says reduced guarding fully exempts the owner, an owner is only liable if he gave no guarding at all. This confirms the case described for him in step 1.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is taught in a ברייתא. This introduces a supporting source.
They are exempt from paying.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: As it is taught: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says:
Both a tam ox and a mu'ad ox
that were given reduced guarding — the owners are exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the case given for רבי אליעזר בן יעקב in step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That according to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, liability requires no guarding at all.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא quoting רבי אליעזר בן יעקב: both a תם and a מועד given reduced guarding are exempt.

steps.title: What רבי יעקב would be teaching about a תם
steps.stepSummary: If the case is a תם, רבי יעקב's new point is that בית דין appoints guardians so that the damages can be collected from the ox's body.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what רבי יעקב teaches us: that בית דין appoints guardians for a תם, in order to collect from its body.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its challenge by showing that reading the case as a תם is not pointless. רבי יעקב would still be teaching something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Paying חצי נזק for a תם seems obvious, so why would רבי יעקב say it? The answer is that the owner here cannot be held responsible, since he is a חרש, שוטה, or קטן. רבי יעקב teaches that בית דין appoints an אפוטרופוס, so the injured person can still collect from the ox itself.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what he teaches us. It shows the new point of a ruling.
Guardians or stewards appointed by בית דין for people who cannot manage their own property.
To collect payment from the ox's own body. This is how damages of a תם are paid.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב –
phrases.english: And this is what Rabbi Yaakov teaches us —
that we appoint guardians for a tam ox,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets ("for them") and some leave it out. The meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: in order to collect from its body.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge by giving the תם reading a real new point.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's need to explain the ruling as a מועד.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Read as a תם, רבי יעקב's ruling is not obvious, because it teaches that guardians are appointed. So the תם reading is fully meaningful.

steps.title: רבא's reading packs two ideas into one ruling
steps.stepSummary: The answer is that רבא explained the case as a מועד because that way רבי יעקב's single ruling contains two ideas from רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: this is what he meant. It is one ruling that has two reasons in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The challenge is answered here. רבא chose the מועד reading on purpose, because then one ruling teaches two ideas.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a מועד, רבי יעקב's ruling of חצי נזק shows two of רבי יהודה's ideas together. First, a מועד still keeps its 'תם part'. Second, reduced guarding is enough for the extra, מועד part. A תם reading would teach less, so the מועד reading is preferred.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he meant. It introduces a clarification of someone's words.
Two reasons, or two ideas.

phrases.english: He said to him: this is what he was saying —
one ruling that contains two reasons.
phrases.notes: He means רבי יעקב's single case of a מועד teaches two of רבי יהודה's ideas at the same time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 1-3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why the מועד reading was preferred even though a תם reading is possible.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since a תם reading works, there seemed no reason to explain the ruling as a מועד.
steps.terutzMaskana: The מועד reading is better because one case teaches two of רבי יהודה's ideas together.

steps.title: רבינא: the argument is about change of custody
steps.stepSummary: רבינא gives a new explanation. רבי יהודה and רבי יעקב argue about whether a change of custody (who is in charge of the ox) changes a מועד ox back into a תם.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: the difference between them is whether a change of custody changes the ox's status. For example, the ox became a מועד while under the guardian, and then the deaf-mute gained his hearing, the mentally incompetent person became competent, or the child grew up. רבי יהודה holds that the ox stays in its old status. רבי יעקב holds that the change of custody changes it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא offers a completely different way to read the argument in the ברייתא. It is no longer about guarding. It is about what happens when the ox goes back to its real owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox became a מועד while a guardian was in charge. Then the owner became able to manage it himself. רבי יהודה says it stays a מועד (בחזקתו), so the owner pays full damage. רבי יעקב says the new owner-in-charge means it goes back to being a תם (רשות משנה), so he pays only חצי נזק.

keyTerms.meaning: A change of ownership or control changes the ox's status.
The practical difference between them is. It points to where two opinions actually split.
It stays in its previous status.
A deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, and a minor. These are people not responsible for their own property.

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to read רבי יעקב. רבא says the case is a מועד, and it shows רבי יהודה's ideas about the 'תם part' and about guarding. רבינא says רבי יעקב and רבי יהודה argue about whether a change of custody (רשות משנה) turns a מועד back into a תם.
steps.confusionAlert: Here 'רשות' does not mean permission. It means whose control or ownership the ox is under.
steps.whyThisMatters: The idea of רשות משנה shows that being מועד can depend on who is in charge of the ox, not only on the ox's behavior.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
The difference between them is whether a change of custody changes the status —
for example, where it became a mu'ad,
and then the deaf-mute gained his hearing,
or the mentally incompetent one became competent,
or the minor grew up.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה סָבַר: הֲרֵי הוּא בְּחֶזְקָתוֹ,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda holds: it remains in its previous status,
Rabbi Yaakov holds: the change of custody changes it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבִינָא אָמַר: רְשׁוּת מְשַׁנָּה אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves רבא's guarding-based explanation and offers a new explanation of the argument.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the point of argument between רבי יהודה and רבי יעקב.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The argument was thought to depend on guarding and on whether a מועד keeps a 'תם part'.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument is about whether a change of ownership returns a מועד to תם status: רבי יהודה says no, רבי יעקב says yes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה: the ox stays מועד. רבי יעקב: רשות משנה, so it goes back to תם and pays חצי נזק.

steps.title: Stewards pay damages but not ransom
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that אפוטרופסים pay damages from the best-quality property, but they do not pay כופר.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: Stewards pay from the best-quality property, but they do not pay ransom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about stewards who manage property, giving them two rules: they pay damages from the best property, but they do not pay כופר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא makes a split. Regular damages are paid by the stewards, and from the best-quality property. The special payment of כופר is not paid. This split sets up the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A steward or guardian who manages property for someone else, such as orphans
Here: the best-quality property or land
Ransom paid by the owner of an ox that killed a person

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
Stewards pay from the best-quality property,
phrases.notes: Literally עלייה means 'upper floor', but here it means the top-quality property.

phrases.english: but they do not pay ransom.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא about stewards, moving past the earlier discussion of guarding and ownership changes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Stewards pay damages from the best property but are exempt from כופר.

steps.title: Who holds that ransom is atonement?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which תנא holds that כופר is atonement, since that would explain why orphans do not pay it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who is the תנא who taught that ransom is atonement, and orphans are not people who need atonement?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks who the author of this ברייתא is. The ברייתא seems to assume that כופר is atonement and that orphans do not need atonement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only reason the ברייתא would exempt from כופר is if כופר is atonement and not just a money payment. Orphans are not held responsible in that way, so they have nothing to atone for. The גמרא wants to find which תנא holds this view of כופר.

keyTerms.meaning: Who is the תנא (the author of this teaching)?
Atonement
Orphans

phrases.english: Who is the one who taught
that ransom is atonement,
and orphans are not people who need atonement?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the author of the ברייתא in step 6, based on its reason for the exemption from כופר.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא holds that כופר is atonement, so that orphans are exempt.

steps.title: רב חסדא names רבי ישמעאל
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says the ברייתא follows רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה. He supports this with a ברייתא where the רבנן say כופר is the victim's value and רבי ישמעאל says it is the damager's value.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: It is רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה. As it was taught: 'Then he shall give the redemption of his life' means the value of the victim. רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה says: the value of the one who caused the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא answers the question by naming רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה. He brings a ברייתא where the רבנן and רבי ישמעאל argue about how much כופר is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא shows a disagreement about the amount of כופר. The רבנן say you pay what the victim was worth. רבי ישמעאל says you pay what the owner of the ox is worth. רב חסדא sees in this a sign that רבי ישמעאל treats כופר as atonement.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
The redemption of his life
The value of the one who was damaged (the victim)
The value of the one who caused the damage

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָה הִיא,
phrases.english: It is Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka,
as it was taught:
'Then he shall give the redemption of his life'
means the value of the victim.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָה אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says:
the value of the one who caused the damage.
phrases.notes: He means the owner of the ox, who is the one responsible.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7 by naming the תנא and citing a ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא follows רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה, who holds that כופר is measured by the damager's value.

steps.title: Their argument is money versus atonement
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the רבנן see כופר as a money payment, while רבי ישמעאל sees it as atonement.
steps.simpleTranslation: What, is it not about this that they argue? The רבנן hold that ransom is a money payment, and רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה holds that ransom is atonement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the ברייתא supports רב חסדא. It suggests that the two opinions are really arguing about what כופר is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If כופר is a money payment for a loss, it makes sense to pay the victim's value, as the רבנן say. If כופר is atonement for the owner's own life, it makes sense to pay his own value, as רבי ישמעאל says. So רבי ישמעאל fits the ברייתא that exempts orphans from כופר.

keyTerms.meaning: What, is it not so that...? (a suggestion the גמרא puts forward)
They argue
Money; a money payment

steps.whatToRemember: This is the suggested reading behind רב חסדא's proof: the רבנן's 'victim's value' means כופר is money, and רבי ישמעאל's 'owner's value' means it is atonement. Step 10 rejects this link.

phrases.english: What, is it not about this that they argue:
that the Rabbis hold:
ransom is a money payment;

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָה סָבַר:
phrases.english: and Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka holds:
ransom is atonement?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the ברייתא cited in step 8, showing why it supports רב חסדא.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה holds כופר is atonement.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא on 'ונתן פדיון נפשו': the victim's value according to the רבנן versus the damager's value according to רבי ישמעאל.

steps.title: רב פפא: everyone agrees ransom is atonement
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rejects the reading from step 9. Both sides agree that כופר is a כפרה. They only argue about whether we measure the value of the נִיזָּק or of the מַזִּיק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: No. Everyone agrees that ransom is atonement. Here they argue about something else. The רבנן hold that we measure the injured person's value. רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה holds that we measure the damager's value.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא pushes back on the idea that the רבנן see כופר as just a money payment. He says the whole argument is only about how to measure the amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 9 the גמרא guessed that 'victim's value' means 'money payment' and 'damager's value' means 'atonement'. רב פפא separates these two questions. Even if כופר is atonement, you still need some way to set the price, and that measuring method is the only point of argument.

keyTerms.meaning: Ransom: the payment an owner makes when his מועד ox kills a person
Atonement
We evaluate or assess (set the value)
The injured or damaged party (here, the person killed)
The damager (here, the ox's owner)
They argue about

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two questions. 'What is כופר?' (atonement) is one question. 'Whose value sets the amount?' is a different one. רב פפא says everyone agrees on the first and argues only about the second.
steps.whyThisMatters: If everyone holds כופר is atonement, then the ברייתא from step 6 (orphans do not pay כופר) fits all opinions. It no longer has to follow רבי ישמעאל alone.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: No;
phrases.notes: 'No' means: the reading from the last step, that the רבנן see כופר as a money payment, is not necessary.

phrases.english: according to everyone, ransom is atonement,
and here they disagree about this:
The Rabbis hold: we evaluate according to the injured party,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָה סָבַר:
phrases.english: and Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, holds:
we evaluate according to the damager.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לָא; דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference in step 9 that the argument is about the nature of כופר.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the inference that the רבנן hold כופר is a money payment. It keeps the ברייתא of the argument itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Measuring by the victim's value does not prove that כופר is a money payment. It can just be the way the atonement amount is set.

steps.title: What is the Rabbis' source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the רבנן measure כופר by the נִיזָּק's value.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the רבנן?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that רב פפא has explained the argument, the גמרא asks for the source of the רבנן's view. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If כופר is atonement for the owner, it seems natural to measure the owner's worth. So the גמרא needs to know why the רבנן measure the victim's worth instead.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason or source?

phrases.english: What is the reasoning of the Rabbis?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the רבנן's position as רב פפא explained it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural basis for measuring כופר by the victim's value.

steps.title: A גזירה שוה from the word 'imposing'
steps.stepSummary: The word 'שִׁיתָה' appears both in the פסוק about כופר and in the פסוק about causing a miscarriage. Payment for a miscarriage is measured by the victim, so כופר is too.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Imposing' is said in the later פסוק, and 'imposing' is said in the earlier פסוק. Just as there it is measured by the injured party, so too here it is measured by the injured party.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the רבנן learn their rule from a גזירה שוה, a link between two פסוקים that use the same word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The כופר פסוק says 'אם כופר יושת עליו'. The earlier פסוק about someone who causes a woman to miscarry says 'כאשר ישית עליו בעל האשה'. In that case the payment is clearly based on the loss of the fetus, the victim. The shared word passes that measuring rule over to כופר.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Imposing' or 'placing': the shared word in the two פסוקים
Below and above: the later and the earlier פסוק in the פרשה
'Just as there, so too here': the standard wording of a comparison

phrases.english: 'Imposing' is stated below,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה on 'שִׁיתָה' links כופר to the miscarriage payment, which is measured by the victim.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל's source: 'the redemption of his life'
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה points to the words 'פִּדְיֹן נַפְשׁוֹ'. The owner is redeeming his own life, so we measure his own value.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה holds: it is written, 'And he shall give the redemption of his life.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the source for the other side, רבי ישמעאל, who measures by the מַזִּיק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'His life' means the owner's life, since he is the one being redeemed. If he is paying for his own life, the price should match his own worth, not the victim's.

keyTerms.meaning: The redemption of his life (his soul)
It is written

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָה סָבַר:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, holds:
'And he shall give the redemption of his life' is written.
phrases.notes: שמות 21:30. 'His life' is the owner's life, so the price follows his worth.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָה סָבַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the opposing view, parallel to the רבנן's source in step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'פִּדְיֹן נַפְשׁוֹ' shows the owner is redeeming his own life, so his own value is measured.

steps.title: The Rabbis accept the פסוק but still measure by the victim
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן agree that the פסוק calls כופר the redemption of the owner's life. Still, the amount is set by the נִיזָּק's value.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן say: Yes, 'the redemption of his life' is written. But when we evaluate, we evaluate according to the injured party.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how the רבנן deal with רבי ישמעאל's פסוק. They accept it, but say it does not decide how to measure the price.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'פִּדְיֹן נַפְשׁוֹ' tells us what כופר is: atonement and redemption for the owner. It does not tell us whose value to measure, and the גזירה שוה settles that question. This fits רב פפא's point that everyone agrees כופר is atonement.

keyTerms.meaning: Yes, indeed
However, nevertheless

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב פפא, everyone agrees כופר is atonement. The רבנן measure it by the victim's value, learned from the גזירה שוה on 'שִׁיתָה'. רבי ישמעאל measures it by the owner's value, learned from 'פִּדְיֹן נַפְשׁוֹ'. The רבנן agree the פסוק calls it redemption, but they still measure by the victim.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis: Yes,
'the redemption of his life' is written;
however, when we evaluate,
we evaluate according to the injured party.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge that רבי ישמעאל's פסוק poses to the רבנן.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the questions: the פסוק defines what כופר is, and the גזירה שוה sets how it is measured.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'פִּדְיֹן נַפְשׁוֹ' would seem to require measuring the owner's own value.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק only shows that כופר is redemption or atonement. The measuring is still by the victim, based on the גזירה שוה.

steps.title: רבא praises רב אחא בר יעקב, and רב נחמן asks to meet him
steps.stepSummary: רבא tells רב נחמן that רב אחא בר יעקב is a great scholar. רב נחמן asks רבא to bring him over when he has the chance.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא was praising רב אחא בר יעקב to רב נחמן, saying he is a great man. רב נחמן said: when he comes to you, bring him to me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a short story that sets up the questions about כופר coming next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No law is taught in this step. It introduces רב אחא בר יעקב as a serious scholar, so we expect his questions to be strong ones.

keyTerms.meaning: praising
a great man (a great scholar)
bring him to me

phrases.english: bring him to my hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story about כופר, after the earlier discussion of how כופר is measured.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling. This is a story that sets up the meeting between רב נחמן and רב אחא בר יעקב.

steps.title: How do two partners pay כופר for their ox?
steps.stepSummary: When רב אחא arrives, רב נחמן invites him to ask a question. He asks how כופר is paid when the ox belongs to two partners.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he came to him, רב נחמן said: Ask me something. He asked: an ox owned by two partners kills a person. How do they pay the כופר?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא בר יעקב asks his first question: how two owners of one ox pay כופר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually one owner pays the כופר. Here there are two owners, so it is unclear how the payment is split. The next step explains why this is hard.

keyTerms.meaning: ask me something
partners
ransom payment for a person killed by a שור מועד

phrases.english: When he came to him,
he said to him: Ask me something.
He asked him:
An ox of two partners,
how do they pay the ransom?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The meeting from the story happens, and the first question is asked.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the כופר payment is divided when an ox has two owners.

steps.title: Neither two full payments nor two half payments seems right
steps.stepSummary: Each partner paying a full כופר is a problem, because the תורה says one כופר. Each partner paying half is also a problem, because the תורה says a full כופר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should each one pay a full כופר? The תורה said one כופר, not two. Should each one pay half? The תורה said a full כופר, not half.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא explains why his question is hard. Both obvious answers seem to go against the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two full payments would mean two כופרים for one death. Two halves means neither owner pays a complete כופר. The difficulty rests on two ideas: there is only one כופר, and each payment should be a full one.

keyTerms.meaning: the Merciful One (the תורה)
one ransom
a full ransom
half a ransom

steps.confusionAlert: This is still part of רב אחא's question, not an answer. He is showing that both choices look wrong. רב נחמן has not answered yet.

phrases.english: Does this one pay a ransom and that one a ransom?
The Merciful One said one ransom,
and not two ransoms!

phrases.aramaic: הַאי חֲצִי כוֹפֶר וְהַאי חֲצִי כוֹפֶר?
phrases.english: This one half a ransom and that one half a ransom?
The Merciful One said a full ransom,
and not half a ransom!

steps.triggerLanguage: כּוֹפֶר אֶחָד אָמַר רַחֲמָנָא, וְלֹא שְׁנֵי כוּפְרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the question in step 16 is hard.
steps.kashyaTarget: Both possible ways for two partners to pay כופר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two full payments break the idea of one כופר. Two halves break the idea of a full כופר.

steps.title: Does בית דין take collateral from someone who owes כופר?
steps.stepSummary: While רב נחמן thinks it over, רב אחא asks a second question. A משנה says we take collateral from people who owe ערכין, but not from people who owe a חטאת or אשם. Which rule applies to כופר?
steps.simpleTranslation: While רב נחמן sat and thought about it, רב אחא said: We learned that we take collateral from people who owe ערכין. We do not take collateral from people who owe a חטאת or an אשם. What about people who owe כופר?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא asks a second question. He uses a משנה to ask whether כופר is treated like a money debt or like a קרבן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה sets up two groups. People who owe ערכין can have collateral taken from them, but people who owe a חטאת or אשם cannot. The question is which group כופר belongs to. That ties back to steps 10-14, where we saw that כופר is a כפרה (atonement) but is also measured like a money payment.

keyTerms.meaning: take collateral (משכון) to force payment
set amounts pledged to the Temple based on a person's age and gender
sin-offerings and guilt-offerings
while he sat and thought it over

steps.whyThisMatters: This question shows the double nature of כופר. It is a payment of money, and it is also a כפרה. That is the same theme from the earlier steps.

phrases.english: While he was sitting and thinking it over,
he said to him: We learned:
phrases.notes: Now רב אחא is speaking again. The משנה is in ערכין כא.

phrases.english: Those who owe valuations: we take collateral from them.
Those who owe sin-offerings and guilt-offerings:
we do not take collateral from them.
Those who owe ransoms, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second question, asked before the first one gets an answer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether בית דין takes collateral from someone who owes כופר, as with ערכין, or does not, as with a חטאת or אשם.

steps.title: The two sides of the collateral question
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא lays out both sides. Maybe כופר is atonement like a חטאת or אשם, so the owner takes it seriously and needs no collateral. Or maybe it is a money payment to another person, so he won't take it seriously and collateral is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since כופר is atonement, maybe it is like a חטאת and an אשם. A person takes those seriously, so there is no need to take collateral from him. Or maybe, since he has to give it to another person, it is just money and not something owed to Heaven. Then he won't take it seriously, and collateral is needed.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא explains why his question about collateral is a real question. He gives a good reason for each side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's rule depends on how seriously a person treats his obligation. A חטאת or אשם brings him atonement, so he wants to bring it and the court doesn't need to push him. כופר is also called atonement, but it is paid to a fellow Jew like a regular debt. So it is unclear which group it belongs to.

keyTerms.meaning: Atonement
Sin-offering and guilt-offering
Collateral, something taken to make sure a debt is paid
The Most High, meaning something owed to Heaven or the מקדש
He surely treats it seriously

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that כופר has two sides. It is a money payment, and it is also called atonement.

phrases.english: Since it is atonement,
it is like a sin-offering and a guilt-offering,
which he certainly treats seriously,
so there is no need to take collateral from him;
or perhaps,
since it is to his fellow
that he must give it,
it is money and not something for the Most High,
so he does not treat it seriously, and we need to take collateral from him?

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן דְּכַפָּרָה הוּא כְּחַטָּאת וְאָשָׁם דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the reasoning behind the question asked in step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Should כופר be grouped with קרבנות (no collateral) or with regular debts (collateral)?

steps.title: Another reason collateral might be needed
steps.stepSummary: There is another way to support the side that requires collateral. The owner did not sin himself; only his property did damage, so he won't take it seriously.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or another reason: he himself did not sin. His property caused the damage. So he doesn't take the matter seriously, and collateral is needed.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא adds a second reason for the side that says we should take collateral.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first reason looked at who receives the payment, which is another person and not Heaven. This reason looks at the owner himself. A חטאת comes for a sin he did, but here only his ox did something. So he may not feel any personal need for atonement.

keyTerms.meaning: Alternatively, or another reason
He sinned
Caused damage

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי, כֵּיוָן דְּהוּא לָא חֲטָא,
phrases.english: Alternatively, since he did not sin,
and it is his property that caused the damage,
the matter is not serious to him,
and we need to take collateral from him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי נָמֵי כֵּיוָן דְּהוּא לָא חֲטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second reason for the second side of the question in step 19.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Same question as step 19, now with a stronger case for taking collateral.

steps.title: רב נחמן is still stuck on the first question
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן asks רב אחא to stop. He is still stuck on the first question about partners.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to him: Leave me alone. I am still stuck on the first question.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן does not answer. He says he has not even solved the first question yet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a real answer. Both of רב אחא's questions are left open here. It shows how hard the questions were, which fits רבא's praise of רב אחא in step 15.

keyTerms.meaning: Leave me alone
I am stuck, I am held up
The first one

steps.whatToRemember: Both of רב אחא's questions stay unanswered here: how two partners pay כופר, and whether we take collateral for כופר.

phrases.english: He said to him: Leave me alone,
I am stuck on the first one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to both questions by saying he has no answer yet.

steps.title: A borrowed ox thought to be a תם turns out to be a מועד
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if someone borrowed an ox thinking it was a תם and it was really a מועד, the owner pays half the damage and the borrower pays half.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: If he borrowed an ox thinking it was a תם, and it turned out to be a מועד, the owner pays half the damage and the borrower pays half the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a ברייתא about a borrowed ox. This sets up the discussion that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a borrower is responsible for damage his borrowed ox does. Here he thought it was a תם, which pays only half. Since it was really a מועד, which pays full damage, the ברייתא splits the payment: half from the borrower and half from the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: The רבנן taught (introduces a ברייתא)
Borrower
An ox not known to gore, which pays half damage
A forewarned ox known to gore, which pays full damage
Half the damage
The owner

steps.confusionAlert: Together the owner and the borrower pay full damage, as a מועד should. The ברייתא only tells us how the payment is split between them.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If he borrowed it on the assumption that it was innocuous,
and it was found to be forewarned,
the owner pays half the damage,
and the borrower pays half the damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן שְׁאָלוֹ בְּחֶזְקַת תָּם וְנִמְצָא מוּעָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the questions about כופר are left open.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A borrowed ox thought to be a תם that turns out to be a מועד: the owner and the borrower each pay half the damage.

steps.title: The ox became dangerous at the borrower's and was returned
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. If the ox became a מועד while with the borrower and was then returned to the owner, the owner pays half damage and the borrower pays nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the ox became a מועד in the borrower's house, and he gave it back to the owner, the owner pays half the damage and the borrower is free from paying anything.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from the last step goes on to the opposite case. Here the ox became a מועד while the borrower had it, and then it went back to the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the owner, the ox still counts as a תם, because it became a מועד while it was not in his hands. So the owner pays only half damage. The borrower pays nothing because the ox is no longer with him.

keyTerms.meaning: It was made a מועד: it gored three times and the person in charge of it (here the borrower) was warned in court
The borrower
The owner
Free from paying anything at all

phrases.english: If it became forewarned in the borrower's house,
and he returned it to the owner,
phrases.notes: The case assumes the ox then gored again after it was back with the owner.

phrases.english: the owner pays half the damage,
and the borrower is exempt from anything.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with the reverse case
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An ox that became a מועד at the borrower's and was returned: the owner pays half damage and the borrower pays nothing.

steps.title: Why should the borrower pay? He borrowed an ox, not a lion
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the first case of the ברייתא again and asks why the borrower pays half. He can tell the owner that he agreed to guard an ordinary ox, not a dangerous 'lion.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: If he borrowed it thinking it was a תם and it turned out to be a מועד, the owner pays half and the borrower pays half. But why? Let the borrower say: I borrowed an ox, I did not borrow a lion!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the ruling from step 22 and challenges it. Why should the borrower pay anything for an ox he never knew was dangerous?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower took the ox believing it was a calm תם. A מועד ox is as dangerous as a lion, and he never agreed to be responsible for that. So it seems he should not have to pay at all.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Master said', used to quote a source again so the גמרא can discuss it
On the assumption that, presumed to be
And why?
A lion

phrases.english: The Master said:
phrases.notes: The גמרא is going back to quote the ברייתא it just brought, so it can ask about it.

phrases.english: If he borrowed it presumed innocuous, and it was found forewarned,

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָלִים מְשַׁלְּמִין חֲצִי נֶזֶק, וְשׁוֹאֵל חֲצִי נֶזֶק.
phrases.english: the owner pays half the damage, and the borrower half the damage.
But why?
Let him say to him:
I borrowed an ox, I did not borrow a lion!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling from step 22 that the borrower pays half
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the borrower pays half damage when the ox turns out to be a מועד
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The borrower only agreed to guard a normal ox. He never took on responsibility for a dangerous one, so he should not pay.

steps.title: רב: the borrower knew it was a gorer
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that the ברייתא is talking about a borrower who knew the ox was a gorer. So he cannot claim he was tricked.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: What case are we dealing with here? A case where the borrower knew the ox was a gorer.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question by narrowing the case. The borrower knew ahead of time that this ox gores.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'I didn't borrow a lion' claim works only if the borrower was surprised. If he knew the ox was a gorer and borrowed it anyway, he accepted that risk, so he shares in paying.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What case are we dealing with here?', used to limit a source to a specific situation
He recognized, he was aware
A gorer, an ox known for goring

phrases.english: Rav said:
Here, with what are we dealing?
Where he was aware of it that it is a gorer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 24
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The borrower had no idea the ox was dangerous, so he could not be held responsible.
steps.terutzMaskana: The borrower knew the ox was a gorer, so he accepted responsibility for its danger.

steps.title: Even so, he borrowed a תם, not a מועד
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on רב. Even if the borrower knew the ox gored, he can say he agreed to guard a תם, not a מועד, which carries full payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him say to the owner: I borrowed a תם, I did not borrow a מועד!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's answer. Knowing the ox gores is still not the same as agreeing to guard a legal מועד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even a borrower who knew the ox was a gorer thought it was legally a תם, where damages are only half. He never agreed to the bigger responsibility of a מועד, so the original question comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But let him say to him', bringing back the borrower's defense
I did not borrow a forewarned ox

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up 'a gorer' with 'a מועד.' An ox can be known to gore and still legally be a תם until it has gored three times and the owner was warned in court.

phrases.english: But let him say to him:
I borrowed an innocuous one, I did not borrow a forewarned one!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's answer in step 25
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's explanation that the borrower knew the ox was a gorer
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Knowing an ox gores still means agreeing only to the risk of a תם. The borrower never took on the full-payment risk of a מועד.

steps.title: The owner says: you would have paid half anyway
steps.stepSummary: The borrower pays half because the owner can tell him that even if the ox were a תם, he would have owed half the damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the owner can say to him: In the end, even if the ox were a תם, you would have had to pay half the damage. So now too, go pay half the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 26. The borrower's complaint does not free him from paying half, because half is exactly what he signed up for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower argued that he only agreed to guard a תם, not a מועד. The answer is that a תם pays חצי נזק, and the ברייתא only makes him pay half. The extra half that comes from the ox being a מועד falls on the owner, not on him.

steps.terutzMaskana: He still pays חצי נזק, the amount he would have owed for a תם. The owner covers the extra half.

steps.title: The borrower says a תם pays only from its own body
steps.stepSummary: The borrower can argue that a תם's half-damage is collected only from the ox itself, not from his own pocket.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let the borrower say to him: If it were a תם, the damage would have been paid from the ox's own body!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 27. It points out that half-damage for a תם is not the same as half-damage paid out of the borrower's own money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The damage from a תם is collected only from the value of the ox that gored. So if the ox were a תם, the borrower's own property would never be touched. Now that it is a מועד, he is being asked to pay from his own money, and that is a real loss for him.

keyTerms.meaning: an ox not yet known to gore, which pays half damage
is paid; is collected
from its body, meaning from the value of the ox itself

phrases.english: But let him say to him:
phrases.notes: Now the borrower is the one talking back to the owner.

phrases.english: If it were a תם, it would have been paid from its body!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְנֵימָא לֵיהּ: אִי תָּם הֲוָה מִשְׁתַּלֵּם מִגּוּפוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 27 that the borrower would have paid half the damage anyway.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A תם's half-damage comes only from the ox's body, not from the borrower's own property. So being made to pay from his own pocket is a new loss he never agreed to.

steps.title: The owner says: you would have repaid me the full ox
steps.stepSummary: The owner answers that the borrower would have had to repay the full value of the ox anyway, so either way the loss is his.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the owner can say to him: In the end, wouldn't you have had to pay me back for my ox?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 28. Even if the damage came from the ox's body, the borrower would have had to make the owner whole for the ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שואל must return the ox to the owner in full. If half the ox's value had been taken to pay the damage, the borrower would have had to make that up to the owner. So the money would come out of his pocket either way, and he loses nothing because the ox turned out to be a מועד.

keyTerms.meaning: ox
to me
a borrower, who must return what he borrowed whole

steps.confusionAlert: The owner is not saying the borrower pays twice. He is saying that in both cases the loss ends up on the borrower, so the source of the payment makes no difference to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the difference the borrower points to makes no real difference, because of his duty to return the ox whole.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Paying from the ox's body would protect the borrower's own money.
steps.terutzMaskana: The borrower would have had to make the owner whole for the ox, so either way the half-damage comes out of his pocket.

steps.title: The borrower prepares another objection
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins one more challenge from the borrower's side. The content of the challenge continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let the borrower say to him:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move: another argument the borrower could make against the owner. The actual argument comes right after this line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same opening phrase from step 28 appears again, which tells us the borrower is pushing back on the answer in step 29. We have to wait for the next line to see exactly what he claims.
